background.definition: Peripheral neuropathy is a general term used to name any dysfunction of one or more parts of the peripheral nervous system. This includes: (1) mononeuropathy, a lesion of one cranial or peripheral nerve (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome); (2) plexopathy, a lesion of a circumscribed part of a brachial or a lumbosacral plexus; (3) radiculopathy, a lesion of a nerve root; and (4) polyneuropathy, a diffuse or multifocal lesions within the peripheral nervous system (e.g., diabetic polyneuropathy). Note that "peripheral neuropathy" is also used in the literature as a synonym for "polyneuropathy," the focus of this chapter.

list.listitem: In clinical research, the most accurate means to diagnose distal-symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP) is the combination of symptoms, signs, and electrodiagnostic testing.

In one study, neurologists elicit causes on 63.5% of patients with DSP on history and physical examination alone. An additional 15.5% were found after laboratory testing. Electrodiagnostic and radio imaging studies rarely resulted in disease-modifying treatment.

Patients presenting with sensory symptoms such as numbness, tingling, pinprick-like, shooting, or burning pain should be evaluated for peripheral neuropathy. The specificity of these symptoms for a diagnosis of diabetic distal-symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP) is about 90%.
A positive family history points to a hereditary neuropathy.
High arches of the feet and hammer toes, consider Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
Using monofilament with a 5.07 Semmes-Weinstein pressure sensation or vibration testing with a 128-Hz tuning fork is the most helpful sensory examination in detecting large fiber neuropathy.
Impaired vibratory detection as a single finding on the examination has moderate (17%-64%) sensitivity and high specificity (>85%) for the presence of polyneuropathy.

The diagnostic value of determining a patient's vibratory detection depends on how it is done. The use of a graded Rydel-Seiffer yields a diagnostic sensitivity for mild polyneuropathy of 76% at a chosen specificity of 95%; sensitivity is lower at the medial malleolus (48%) and ulnar styloid (29%).
Decreased or absent ankle reflexes as a single finding on the examination are of moderate (60%-80%) sensitivity and high specificity (>90%) for the presence of polyneuropathy.
These symptoms and signs are typically presented in a glove and stocking distribution.

A measure of blood sugar is the most important laboratory test in a patient presenting with a slowly progressive polyneuropathy. Prediabetes, as identified by an abnormal oral glucose tolerance test, is found in 62% of patients with chronic axonal polyneuropathy of unknown cause.

Further recommended laboratory testing for most patients with persistent peripheral neuropathy includes CBC, serum electrolytes, BUN, hepatic transaminases, vitamins B1 and B12, serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) with immunofixation, TSH, ESR, serum angiotensinconverting enzyme (to rule out sarcoid), and tests for HIV and Lyme diseases. Also, test urine for protein.

Of these tests, fasting blood sugar, vitamin B12 level (confirmed by methylmalonic acid and homocysteine) and SPEP have the highest yield and are recommended for evaluation of distal sympathetic polyneuropathy (DSP) by American Academy of Neurology.
Nerve conduction studies (NCS) are frequently recommended as the major diagnostic test for peripheral neuropathy.

NCS are used to classify a peripheral neuropathy as axonal, demyelinating, or both. This distinction helps in identifying the etiology. If the neuropathy is primary demyelinating, large numbers of rare disorders are potential causes.

Skin biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy that solely or predominantly affects unmyelinated sensory nerve fibers ("small fiber neuropathy"). Punch biopsy with a 3-mm instrument is generally recommended.
Nerve biopsy is not helpful if used only for the detection of a peripheral neuropathy.
In patients with cryptogenic polyneuropathy and a familial pattern of inherited neuropathy, consider genetic testing.

If these tests all are normal in a patient with chronic axonal polyneuropathy, treatable causes of the neuropathy are unlikely, and a diagnosis of CIAP is supported. If one or more tests are abnormal, this should point to the etiology of the neuropathy.
Rate-dependent depression of the Hoffmann (H) wave may be valuable for predicting the initial efficacy of gabapentin therapy in patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy
Consider peripheral neuropathy in patients with sensory symptoms such as numbness, tingling, pinprick-like pain.
With a distal-symmetric pattern of the symptoms and with decreased or absent ankle reflexes and decreased distal sensation, a distal-symmetric polyneuropathy is likely.
In most patients, the etiology cannot be inferred from the signs and symptoms. NCS can help to establish a diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy and may assist in determining the etiology.
A suggested diagnostic strategy for patients with distal-symmetric polyneuropathy is given in .
If the signs and symptoms develop acutely (within 4 weeks), an inflammatory or a toxic etiology is likely. Immediate referral for specialized neurological care is warranted. C
In patients with asymmetrical sensory loss, motor neuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, consider consulting a neurologist. C
Urgent hospitalization is recommended in a patient with motor neuropathy and concern for respiratory compromise. C

First-line treatment for neuropathic pain includes anticonvulsants; gabapentin/pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, consensus recommendation. See chapter on management of Diabetic Neuropathy for additional detail A

Adults with painful diabetic neuropathy had similar degrees of improvement with monotherapy using amitriptyline, duloextine, and pregabalin. However, there was even greater improvement with subsequent combination therapy regardless of initial choice of medication.
